So we've all seen this movie before where companies that do well start to get out of their lane a bit too much. They think they're just like the hottest startups and maybe they have some good things going, but they don't really know how hard it is to keep up with the leaders at scale. But I'm surprised because one recent deal seems pretty egregious even by these standards, and that's Capital One buying Brex for $5.15 billion. And Brex had raised at a $12.3 billion valuation. That means Brex is selling for roughly half what they raised at. Now, Brex is still growing very quickly. So if they were able to sell at double triple digit growth, that would make sense. It might be worth more than twice what they raised at. But I bet it wasn't. Because there's a big difference between growing fast and growing hyper fast. If you look back at public software stocks today, the ones that can grow over 50%, 60% that have high margins are trading multiples of 10 times revenues, sometimes higher. The ones that aren't quite there trade at lower multiples. But none of them are at 300 x ARR. None of them are at 200 x ARR. Most importantly, none of them are at 700 x ARR. Which is exactly where Brex had been valued. Now, that does seem nuts now looking back. We'll see. Maybe they hit those valuations again. But it seemed nuts at the time. So my advice is, just remember that capital markets are unforgiving. A few months ago, AI agents were unstoppable. Today, Salesforce laid off 800 people. It's not all sunshine and rainbows. Make sure you understand why the market thinks your business is great.

Q:
How does a messy cap table affect future investors and fundraising?
A messy cap table can make fundraising much harder because many investors want clean ownership structures. It may also create conflicts between existing shareholders who don't get along with each other. But if you already know how to navigate these dynamics, you might just ignore it. Some VCs will care less about this stuff if they think their investment will still work out regardless.

How does a messy cap table affect future investors and fundraising? If a company doesn't have a super clean cap table (i.e., no one owns >15%), it will likely limit their ability to raise capital from new investors. Founders need to do everything they can to ensure their cap table reflects them being the majority owners going into any potential fundraise. Otherwise, it can hurt their chances with VCs. In fact, most founders don't understand how sensitive VCs are to dilution -- so many things they might want to do actually end up killing all hope of raising another round. For example, selling shares to yourself after a round is generally OK if you're still early stage. But try to sell too much, or too soon after the last round, and you'll make most VCs run the other way. I've seen this happen again and again, especially when folks get a little desperate. And what about "dilutive" SAFE notes or convertible debt? Well, in theory these aren't dilutive until converted. But in practice, most VCs just assume they will convert, and thus take some ownership. So ask how much ownership you'd be giving up before signing anything. That should save you a lot of headaches, and maybe save a few bridges. What else hurts? - Selling stock options to employees in rounds where there is very low demand. This creates far more dilution than intended. - Not keeping the original price per share / SAFEs/convertible note same for every investor. It sends the wrong signal. - Taking out loans or SAFE Notes to
How does a messy cap table affect future investors and fundraising?

So what happens with this cap table when we're going out to raise again?
Well first, you're gonna hear all sorts of different answers from VCs, especially from seed stage VCs.
Some will say, "Oh, well, it doesn't really matter."
And then some will say, "I don't want to do anything with them because they just did something terrible like they gave away too much equity."
But here's my take after seeing so many founders go through this:
It matters less if you haven't raised since that crazy deal happened, but it still matters a lot if you've been raising since.
In fact, I would advise against anyone raising any new capital ever after having done one of these crazy deals.
Once you start raising, once you have a clean cap table, no one wants to see a big chunk of the ownership going somewhere else.
That's why I try to tell every founder I work with, "Just keep your cap table simple until you're ready to raise again."
Because you'll get more offers, you'll get more interest if there aren't weird things in the cap table.
This is true with any type of financing, whether it's debt or equity.
No investor likes to see their dollars being used inefficiently by dilution outside of the company.
Especially venture capitalists, who need to make sure that every single share that gets issued goes into their pockets in order to create liquidity.
So yeah, you know, that's my advice.
And also, I think a related piece of advice is never, never, never run out of money.
Never let yourself fall into a position where you're default dead without a term sheet in hand.
There are exceptions, right?
Like if you have enough cash that you're confident you could cut costs dramatically and extend your runway.
But most VCs won't invest in companies they feel are default dead.
They'll pass.
Even though they might think you're great, they just won't fund someone whose runway is zero days.
Or close to it.
So I always tell folks, you gotta be careful running out of money.
It leads to bad decisions. It creates chaos. And ultimately, it ends up killing startups.

So I did want to step back on this because one thing we know is almost everyone in B2B software now wants to use AI to personalize the customer experience more than ever before. We talked to an incredible CMO recently who literally just left her job, she'd been running marketing at a very successful unicorn for years. She came out swinging in our podcast like she hasn't seen anything better than ChatGPT for personalization. That's how excited she is. But what does that really mean? Is every single interaction with your product going to have to be personalized? Can they all be done through a chatbot and a prompt? A lot of folks think so. So I wanted to see if I could find where this first originated. It seems like such a great idea. Everyone loves personalization. They're good at it when they have lots of humans and can do it manually, but even there, customers complain they don't get enough attention. What would happen if we could magically deliver that to each and every customer, no matter how small, no matter how large, with a prompt? The originator here I believe was the founder of Rippling, Parker Conrad. He wrote a pretty interesting article on his thoughts on the future of enterprise SaaS after attending SaaStr Annual. He gave us some great content. He had some great insights. One of them was, "I've decided the future of business software is to make it hyper-personalized." Now, I'm sure many of you love the word "hyperpersonalized" because it sounds cool. But actually, it's probably already been achieved by many of your competitors. Rippling's vision here is that AI will allow companies to build exactly what customers want -- customized workflows, tailored experiences, and automated processes all without needing to code.

So my general advice on hiring a new VP of Sales is this: - First ask if they can truly hit plan in 90 days with just their small team (not including any internal resources). If they can't — pass. They don't really understand your business. You need someone that can get you to first $Xm faster than now. - Next, ask how many quota-hitting reps they've directly managed before. And make sure those quota-hitters were individual contributors / SDRs >and< closers. Not just "managers" or people that didn't close anything themselves. If they haven't hired at least 1-2 strong quota-closing reps for real themselves... then I doubt they ever did. - Finally, ask what % of their revenue was closed by folks that worked for them directly. Ask for the number. It almost always turns out < 50%. So no matter how much talk there is here -- the best VPs of Sales hire folks that already know how to sell the product. But importantly, that's often just 25%-30% of their team. The rest of their team is made up of folks that want to learn how to sell the product. This ratio usually changes over time, as the company grows and scales. At some point, most of the sales team will have been trained by folks that used to report to the VP of Sales. So there’s no easy way to know exactly what happened here because all I have access to is this tweet:
Capital One announced today they will acquire Brex for $5.15 Billion
CEO & Founder Sam Blond announced his departure effective immediately
pic.twitter.com/FsQ9pNkFJt
— Myles Hatz (@M_Hatz)
February 10, 2026
It looks like it was $5.15 Billion.  That’s what Capital One said.  But Brex itself wasn’t clear.  It just said “terms were agreed” in a release.  We don’t really know yet if it was truly $5 Billion (with some cash), $5.15 Billion, etc.  Or even how much cash vs stock was involved.
What we do know is a few things … First, Brex had raised at $12.3 Billion pre-money valuations (Oct ’22) then fell dramatically during the downturn to < $1 Billion (!).  So whatever deal they got would likely be far lower than its peak valuation.
Second, it doesn’t look like anyone in the public markets thought Brex could get anywhere close to a $12B exit anymore.  Even at ~$600m ARR, getting even a $1B+ exit was probably seen by many as a stretch given current multiples.  The market cap of public companies doing similar things like Ramp, Navan, etc. aren’t trading anywhere near where Brex peaked at a $12B valuation.
Third, Brex isn’t the first startup to see the bar go up during the downturn.  And fourth, it shows how tough times can lead to founder departures.  Not always a bad thing per se, but often not fun for everyone.  A bit more on that
here
.
And a reminder that while VCs want founders who win, they also need them to survive long enough to have something left over for investors.  Sometimes that means letting folks go to focus resources on survival and growth.

So we've all seen this movie play out again and again across B2B. A startup raises a bunch of money at a crazy high valuation and then they get bought by a big tech company for … much less than the headline number. It happened with Bill.com, it happened with Clio, it happened with Veeva. And now I think it just happened again with Brex and Capital One. So what actually happened here?
Capital One announced an agreement to acquire Brex for roughly $5.15 billion. But if you dig into how that deal got structured, the actual story gets pretty interesting. Brex raised over a billion dollars at a valuation north of twelve billion dollars back in late 2021. This is where things start to go sideways because raising at such an extreme multiple means there's no margin for error. You're basically counting on top decile performance every single year for years and years. Fast forward to today, and the math doesn't work anymore. The company reportedly generated approximately $300 million in revenue in 2024. At even modest multiples, that would value the business well below the five point two billion announced purchase price. Now let me share something that might sound obvious but bear with me because it matters. When companies like this sell early – whether through acquisition or IPO – founders often frame it as "winning" regardless of the ultimate financial outcome. They'll say they created hundreds of millions in wealth for employees, investors, and themselves. They'll point to their legacy, their impact on the market, their ability to attract top talent. All those points are valid. But the reality is more complicated.

So this was an interesting thread on LinkedIn over the past few days I thought worth summarizing, just some learnings.
And so there’s two pieces of advice, really, two big things you can do to increase your odds of making better hires when you’re hiring VPs, directors, whatever it is. And it turns out they go together. But they go against conventional wisdom today. So the first piece of advice is hire folks who are still hands-on, still do the work themselves. This seems obvious for junior hires, but less so for more senior ones. But we know it’s true, right? We all know it’s true. You want someone running sales ops to also be able to code up a dash board. Someone managing engineering to also ship product. Or something like that. That’s obviously important for junior roles. But what about senior leadership?
I think most founders would agree, sort of. They’d say yes, they want their senior leaders to still be able to roll up their sleeves, even if sometimes they don’t need to anymore. But here’s my learning:
if you hire someone to lead sales whose last experience wasn’t building a team, leading from the front—then they probably won’t succeed. Same thing for marketing. For support. Whatever it is. Now I’m not saying you shouldn’t hire people that aren’t technical. Because if you haven’t done it yourself, you’re not going to understand how hard it is. But if someone hasn’t done it recently themselves—you’re making a bet. It might pay off. It might not. But it’ll never make sense. Especially if you’re below $250m in revenue. Because these execs that haven’t done it for a while … well … they’ve lost touch. They’re been away too long. They forget what it takes. They start talking about strategy instead of execution. And that’s death at a startup. The second point I wanted to share is this.

AI will also have a personalization layer on top of it so we can talk to it like ChatGPT or Claude where I don't know every single feature in Asana so if I say "I want to track my time better" it would understand what I mean and make some suggestions to help me do that versus just saying "Hey here's how you use the timer."
What does that look like in practice? Well, there is this concept called "intents." So, when you're using the app, you'll tell it what your intent is, and then the system will go through different pieces of code that try to fulfill those intents. That way, you won't need to navigate through multiple places. It'll just take care of it for you. The second piece is more around understanding who your users are, which we've talked a lot about, right? How do you really get to know them, how do you really personalize for them? Because right now, you're talking to a persona, not a real human being. There are so many personas in a company. There are 500 people. You might think that one team uses Slack, another team uses Microsoft Teams, and they all use something else. But actually, everyone uses Slack because they don't even know anything else. They just use whatever tool is available to them. So, making sure that our products deeply understand who our customers are and why they buy us, why they choose us over others, is super important.

There is no point doing anything less than perfect when you hire your VP of Sales. It's just too important. So if they don't hit the plan their first month, fire them. If they aren't recruiting strong folks under them by Month 2, fire them. If they can't close every big deal themselves -- even when they lose -- by Month 2, fire them. And importantly, criticize them mercilessly until then for failing. Because most won't deliver, period. They'll blame others. Blame marketing for lack of leads. Blame product for being feature poor. Blame anyone else except for themselves for not hitting the plan. But what you really need to do is help them succeed. Help them get there. This is also why I've never made this mistake myself hiring sales leaders. We all make mistakes. The key isn't making fewer mistakes (you're going to). It keeps going. So, if everything works, eventually you might even sell your company for billions of dollars, which means your parents will become billionaires overnight. Now, the thing that complicates this whole process is something called dilution. Dilution happens every time you raise another round of funding. So let me explain it. If I were to buy five percent of your company today and your company was worth say, $100 million, then my stake would also be worth five percent times $100 million, which equals $5 million. The problem is, later, you decide you need some extra capital. So you decide to raise another round of venture financing, but you ask the new investors to pay a lot less per share than what I paid. This means I'm left holding shares of your company that aren't worth very much anymore. In fact, I'd lose my entire initial $5 million investment. So there was an interesting discussion on our Twitter / LinkedIn this week on whether CEOs need to be hands-on in their business, or if they can just sort of manage and have the best people under them report up to them. It’s hard to measure this exactly. But intuitively, one would think so. So when I see a CEO hire a bunch of VPs early, without ever having even been a VP themselves … that worries me. When I see someone join the board of directors of a company before they’ve truly built something themselves … that worries me. There are exceptions, clearly. Criticizing a VP of Sales who cannot do better is counterproductive
https://t.co/8cYlOq0HkV

As I’ve shared many times on SaaStr over the years, hiring a “wrong fit” VPS can end up costing you almost as much as if you’d never hired anyone at all.  If they don’t work out, and you just let things slide … it’s hard to get back to where you were before.
But what happens when your new VPS does OK — for a while? But then doesn’t really grow your revenue anymore?
Should you criticize him or her, point fingers, make demands? Or will that hurt morale even further? I.e., can you ever move forward past this stage?
I’m not sure there’s a simple answer. Let me share my learnings here:
First, some bad VPs of Sales will take advantage of time. They’ll promise to hire their top reps, but won’t actually do so. So yes, they’ll look good initially — at first. Then later, they’ll have zero people left underperforming. Which often looks even worse than before. Don’t play these games. It always ends badly. Instead, find someone else to replace any failing sales execs asap. Second, sometimes it’s best to just agree to disagree on performance issues. Sometimes, a VP of Sales will push back on how many leads she needs per rep, or how big an ACV she can close, etc. There’s nothing wrong with pushing back against an unrealistic goal set by management. But it also doesn’t help if you argue too much here. Instead, just agree on goals that are achievable given the current state of the company. Third, don’t expect miracles from a mediocre VP of Sales.

So my top mistakes hiring VPs of Sales … - Hiring too early (e.g., when you have fewer than 10 customers) - Not being careful enough about references - Being overly impressed by logos / brands - Not doing enough diligence on domain expertise - Hiring reps I wouldn't buy from myself - Expecting magic vs reality - Firing before you know if they can really scale - Ignoring signs you've made a mis-hire too long

So I've talked on SaaStr for years now about hiring a great VP of Sales. How to hire her. What mistakes you make when you don't find a good one. But there were two points that we didn't dig into too much. And so let me just quickly summarize those today because they're super important if you haven't figured this out yet. Number one, don't criticize your VPS. Don't tear him apart over the internet. If she can't get it done, then move on. But don't criticize her publicly. Because that is almost always counterproductive. It undermines their confidence. It undermines morale. In fact, most VPs will quit after public criticism. So instead, what you need to do is backfill him. Help him. And if you have to go another month, you'll survive. Your revenue will still grow. It won't kill you. But tearing someone down doesn't help anyone. Number two, folks want to know whether or not a great VP of Sales needs to bring in all these reps under them. Can they really do it alone? Well, yes and no. Yes, if it's early stage, maybe start off with just one rep yourself. Maybe even zero. If it's later stage, well then probably you need three to four reps in the first week or two. And a VP of Sales that wants to work themselves up from nothing, well, they might be able to do that. They might want to put in the effort. But that's rare. It's very hard to do it without any experience. And ultimately, if you want to scale faster than 10x, you're going to need to hire ahead of time. We've also learned since Covid that folks aren't as interested in working remotely anymore. Many VPs of Sales, many CROs want to manage reps in the office. They want to fly around.

Capital One just announced it will acquire Brex, a fintech start-up, for approximately $5.2 billion in cash.

And boy did they bet big.  A lot bigger than anyone could imagine today.  A lot bigger than even their $10B round suggested would ever happen — back then.  Back when many thought AI would save us all, back when everyone wanted to invest everywhere, anywhere.

Q:
How does a messy cap table affect future investors and fundraising?
A messy cap table can make fundraising much harder because many investors want clean ownership structures. It may also create conflicts between existing shareholders who don't get along with each other. But if you already know how to navigate these dynamics, you might just ignore all this and go ahead and raise whatever you need — if you need it fast.

What Does The Pilot Source Say Happens To Executives Who Stay Close To The Craft?
There isn’t any information in the prompt about “the pilot source,” so I’ll answer based on what we know about successful founders:
Executives who stay close to the craft win, while those who become pure managers and strategists lose. As you scale, there’s always a temptation for execs to step back and let others handle the day-to-day details. But if you’re going after truly innovative markets like AI, staying close to customers and product development is often where the magic happens. Remember when most folks got laid off at scale-ups during Covid? Yes, it was rough. But also … everyone went remote. And it became clear quickly which ones could thrive without the office. Those were the ones that stayed closer to their customers. Now many of us want to go back to offices, but the same dynamic holds true today. Folks that really get the value proposition and can solve problems better tend to perform best in sales and engineering. They don’t just manage people well — they sell themselves. They know how to ship code and build products faster than ever before. If you’re building something revolutionary, surround yourself with people who aren’t afraid to roll up their sleeves and get their hands dirty. Don’t hire a team of pure managers – they won’t help you win the game.

Who said that AI means everything in SaaS needs to be a personalized experience?
Anneka Gupta
AI will also have an impact on how we think about personalization. We’re already seeing this happen with ChatGPT where users can create custom personas like Jason’s “Boring Sales Guy” character. But there’s more beyond just creating characters. I’m going to predict that the next level of AI innovation is going to be around the ability for customers to customize the way they want to interact with your app—whether through voice, chatbot, mobile, whatever it might be—and get a completely customized view of what they want to see based on those interactions. So whether it’s creating different avatars within an application, or allowing customers to choose how they want to interact with your product, I believe that’s going to be a really exciting area of opportunity for us to explore in the future.

And also you can't really criticize him if he hires mediocre folks — they will always blame him for their failures
So if you see this, try to help instead.
